evidence_chain: Fact: Cohu describes itself as a global technology leader supplying test, automation, inspection and metrology products and services to the semiconductor industry. Source: https://ir.cohu.com/

Fact: Cohu states it is a leading supplier of semiconductor test handlers and contactors and a growing provider of automated test equipment, inspection & metrology solutions, and data analytics software. Source: https://ir.cohu.com/

Fact: Cohu’s website says its solutions support artificial intelligence, high-performance computing, automotive and autonomous systems, advanced medical equipment, and global connectivity. Source: https://cohu.com/

Fact: Cohu’s product portfolio includes equipment used to automate semiconductor device movement, control temperature during test, provide vision inspection, support ATE, provide contactors, and deliver AI-driven analytics for semiconductor manufacturers. Source: https://cohu.com/

Fact: Cohu’s investor-relations page listed an April 2, 2026 press release titled 'Cohu Announces $30 Million Follow-On Orders for High-Performance Computing Test.' Source: https://cohu.gcs-web.com/investor-relations

Fact: Cohu’s investor-relations page listed a May 12, 2026 press release titled 'Cohu Receives Multiple Orders for Testing Next-Generation GaN Power Devices for AI Data Centers.' Source: https://ir.cohu.com/

Fact: Public company-profile data describes Cohu as supplying test and inspection metrology automation systems, MEMS test modules, test contactors, thermal subsystems, data analytics software, ATE, handlers, interface products, probe heads and pins, and related services. Source: https://stockanalysis.com/stocks/cohu/company/

Inference: Because AI/HPC and HBM devices increase package complexity, power density, signal-integrity requirements, and thermal constraints, back-end handling, contact, inspection, metrology, and thermal test may become more important chokepoint layers.
Hypothesis: Cohu’s AI/HBM-related products could become material enough to change investor perception if order flow, revenue mix, bookings, backlog, and margins show sustained AI/HPC contribution.

Unverified item: The provided evidence does not yet quantify Neon, Eclipse, HBM inspection, or AI/HPC handler revenue as a percentage of total company revenue; this must be checked in the latest 10-K, 10-Q, transcript, and investor presentation.
falsification_plan: Downgrade the thesis if the latest 10-K, 10-Q, earnings call, or investor deck does not contain meaningful references to HBM, AI, HPC, Neon, Eclipse, contactors, thermal test, inspection/metrology, or related product wins.
Falsify the upgrade case if HBM inspection and AI/HPC handler/contact/thermal-test products remain unquantified and immaterial for several quarters despite management commentary.
Downgrade if bookings fail to recover or backlog does not expand after announced HPC or AI data-center-related orders.
Downgrade if gross margin does not improve, or management attributes margin pressure to underutilization, pricing, or unfavorable mix despite AI/HPC product claims.
Falsify if legacy automotive, industrial, mobility, or broad semiconductor weakness continues to dominate revenue and margins, with no evidence of AI/HPC offset.
Downgrade if competitors announce more visible HBM inspection, handler, contactor, or thermal-test wins at major memory, foundry, logic, or OSAT customers.
Falsify if repeat orders do not follow initial AI/HPC or GaN AI data-center test announcements.
Downgrade if customer qualifications are delayed, cancelled, or limited to engineering samples rather than production-volume deployments.
deep_reports.hidden_signal_to_verify: The key hidden signal is whether HBM inspection and AI/HPC-related handler, contactor, thermal-test, ATE, or metrology products are moving from isolated design wins and small product-level orders into a recurring, material revenue stream. Specific upgrade evidence would include quantified HBM/AI/HPC revenue, repeat orders, backlog expansion, customer qualification for next-generation HBM or high-power AI/HPC packages, gross-margin uplift from mix, and management commentary that AI/HPC growth is offsetting weakness in automotive, industrial, mobility, or legacy semiconductor test.

Create an evidence upgrade ladder: Level 1 equals product mentions; Level 2 equals named order categories; Level 3 equals repeat orders/backlog; Level 4 equals quantified AI/HBM revenue; Level 5 equals margin and company-level revenue inflection.
risks: Materiality risk: AI/HBM-related products may remain too small to move total revenue, bookings, gross margin, or operating leverage.
Cycle risk: weakness in automotive, industrial, mobility, or legacy semiconductor test may overwhelm AI/HPC product growth.
Disclosure risk: management may discuss AI/HPC design wins without quantifying revenue, backlog, customer concentration, or margin impact.
Competitive risk: larger or more specialized test, handler, inspection, contactor, or metrology competitors may capture the main HBM and AI/HPC opportunities.
Qualification risk: AI/HPC and HBM production flows require customer qualification; delays, failed qualifications, or lack of repeat orders would weaken the thesis.
Margin risk: high-complexity products may not improve gross margin if pricing pressure, underutilization, integration costs, or service burden offsets mix benefits.
Narrative risk: the stock may already begin to price AI/HPC optionality before product-level evidence is strong enough, reducing the underfollowed edge.
Customer-concentration risk: a small number of AI/HPC or HBM customers could drive orders, creating volatility if programs pause or switch suppliers.
Technology-substitution risk: changes in package architecture, test flow, inspection method, or in-house customer capability could reduce Cohu’s attach rate.
Evidence-quality risk: current evidence supports exposure and order signals, but not yet a fully proven company-level AI/HBM revenue transition.
deep_reports.supply_chain_position: AI supply chain node: downstream AI accelerators and HBM devices -> semiconductor manufacturing and OSAT/back-end process flow -> package/device inspection, metrology, handler automation, contactor interface, thermal control during test, ATE, process-control analytics -> Cohu as a supplier of semiconductor test automation, interface/contactors, inspection & metrology, ATE, thermal subsystems, and analytics. This is one to two steps away from the headline AI accelerator/HBM beneficiaries, making it a second-order chokepoint candidate rather than a direct AI compute supplier.
deep_reports.thesis_cn: 假设：AI/HPC 芯片与 HBM 器件的复杂度提升，会提高后段测试、检测、分选、接触器、热管理测试和计量环节的重要性。Cohu 被市场更多视为传统半导体测试设备、汽车和工业周期敞口公司，因此其 AI/HBM 相关产品线可能被低估。若 Neon、Eclipse、HBM inspection、AI/HPC handler、contactors、thermal test 或相关平台从小基数增长为可见收入，并能抵消传统市场疲弱，Cohu 的叙事可能从周期性测试设备供应商切换为 AI 半导体后段基础设施供应商。当前结论级别仍是 hypothesis，因为已知公开信号显示公司有 AI/HPC、test handling、contactors、inspection/metrology、thermal subsystems 和 data analytics 相关业务，但尚需验证产品级收入、订单、客户复购和毛利率贡献是否足够大。
deep_reports.thesis_en: Hypothesis: rising complexity in AI/HPC devices and HBM may increase the importance of back-end semiconductor test, inspection, handling, contactors, thermal test, and metrology. Cohu is often screened as a cyclical semiconductor test equipment supplier with automotive and industrial exposure, so the market may under-recognize its AI/HBM-linked product optionality. If Neon, Eclipse, HBM inspection, AI/HPC handlers, contactors, thermal test, or related platforms scale from small bases into visible revenue and offset legacy-market weakness, Cohu could be reframed as an AI back-end semiconductor infrastructure supplier. This remains a hypothesis, not a confirmed thesis: public evidence supports Cohu’s presence in test handlers, contactors, ATE, inspection/metrology, thermal subsystems, analytics, AI/HPC, and recent HPC/GaN AI data-center orders, but company-level materiality, product revenue, repeat orders, and margin contribution still need verification.

deep_reports.why_underfollowed: Cohu is commonly categorized as a semiconductor equipment and test-handler supplier with cyclical exposure to automotive, industrial, mobility, and broader semiconductor capex. The AI signal is hidden at the product and customer-qualification level rather than in headline GPU, cloud, or accelerator revenue. The market may miss it because the relevant indicators are specific order announcements, product-family adoption, HBM/AI/HPC handler qualifications, contactor usage, thermal-test requirements, inspection/metrology attach rates, and mix-driven margin changes rather than simple AI revenue disclosure.

evidence.claim: Cohu is a public semiconductor test, automation, inspection, metrology, and services supplier.
Cohu says it is a leading supplier of semiconductor test handlers and contactors and a growing provider of ATE, inspection/metrology, and data analytics software.
Cohu’s solutions support artificial intelligence and high-performance computing among other applications.
Cohu’s portfolio includes device movement automation, temperature control during test, vision inspection, ATE, contactors, and AI-driven analytics.
Cohu’s investor-relations site listed an April 2, 2026 announcement for $30 million follow-on orders for high-performance computing test.
Cohu’s investor-relations site listed a May 12, 2026 announcement for multiple orders testing next-generation GaN power devices for AI data centers.

Cohu supplies test and inspection metrology automation systems, MEMS test modules, test contactors, thermal subsystems, data analytics software, ATE, handlers, interface products, probe heads and pins, spares, warranties, training, and software/services.
Cohu’s AI/HBM thesis is a second-order bottleneck thesis rather than a direct AI accelerator revenue thesis.
The current evidence is not yet sufficient to prove that AI/HBM-related products are material to total company revenue or margins.

memory_update.value: Underfollowed AI/HBM back-end semiconductor infrastructure candidate. Maintain as hypothesis pending verification of product-level materiality, repeat orders, backlog, and gross-margin contribution.
Watch whether HBM inspection, AI/HPC handlers, contactors, thermal test, ATE, metrology, Neon, Eclipse, and GaN AI data-center test orders become quantified, recurring, and material.

Downgrade if AI/HBM/HPC product signals remain unquantified or immaterial, bookings/backlog fail to improve, legacy weakness overwhelms growth, or competitors capture the key HBM/AI-HPC test opportunities.

summary: Layer 5 mini deep report for one underfollowed AI target: Cohu (COHU). Core hypothesis: AI/HBM growth may create a second-order bottleneck in back-end semiconductor inspection, test handling, contactors, thermal test, and metrology. The thesis is not yet proven at company scale; it requires verification that HBM/AI/HPC products such as Neon, Eclipse, contactors, thermal test, inspection/metrology, or related platforms are becoming material enough to offset legacy automotive/industrial/cyclical semiconductor weakness.
